Infectious/inflammatory conditions; Possible neoplastic involvement in older adults
May be tender if reactive or firm and nonâ€tender if neoplastic; Often associated with systemic signs in infection (fever, malaise)

Initial antibiotic therapy for suspected infection; Excisional biopsy or further imaging if nodes persist
Exclude malignancy with FNAC and, if needed, core biopsy; Use imaging to differentiate from cystic lesions (e.g. thyroglossal cyst)

Dermoid Cyst
Benign congenital cyst composed of ectodermal elements
Embryologic sequestration of skin and adnexal structures during development

Exclude abscess formation using imaging characteristics (lack of systemic infection signs); Rule out cystic lesions by the presence of inflammatory fluid rather than a true cyst wall
Recurrence if underlying overuse is not addressed; Infection if the fluid collection becomes superinfected
Ranula
Mucous extravasation cyst arising from a disrupted sublingual gland duct
Trauma or idiopathic disruption of the salivary duct
Bluish, transilluminating, cystic swelling on the floor of the mouth; Typically located lateral to the midline
Ultrasound identifies a cystic lesion in the sublingual region; MRI for complex or recurrent cases
Excision or marsupialization combined with identification/treatment of the affected gland

Small, domeâ€shaped, mobile nodule that may become inflamed if secondarily infected
Ultrasound shows a wellâ€circumscribed, cystic lesion with possible internal debris
Simple surgical excision when indicated, particularly for recurrent inflammation
Exclude inflamed abscess by noting absence of systemic signs; Differentiate from lipoma by firmness and imaging characteristics
Recurrence with incomplete excision; Occasional infection requiring antibiotic treatment
Lipoma
Benign tumor of adipose tissue presenting as a soft neck mass
Idiopathic; Occasional familial tendency
Soft, mobile, and painless mass with slow growth
Ultrasound reveals a hyperechoic, homogeneous lesion; MRI for further tissue characterization if indicated

Branchial Cleft Anomalies (Cyst/Fistula)
Congenital malformation from failure of branchial cleft obliteration

Presents as a lateral cyst, sinus, or fistula usually along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle; May leak fluid or become secondarily infected

Cervical Rib

Diseases of Function (Hyperthyroidism & Hypothyroidism)

Hyperthyroidism: tremor, palpitations, sweating, weight loss; Hypothyroidism: lethargy, weight gain, cold intolerance
TFTs (TSH, T3, T4) show hormone imbalances; Ultrasound to evaluate gland size and detect nodules
Hyperthyroidism: beta blockers and antithyroid agents; Hypothyroidism: lifelong thyroxine replacement with dose titration based on TSH levels
Exclude destructive thyroiditis by serial hormone testing and inflammatory markers; Use imaging to rule out nodular causes when gland function is normal
Cardiac arrhythmias in hyperthyroidism; Myxedema and metabolic slowdown in hypothyroidism
Disorders of Size (Simple Goitre, nSTN, nMNG)
Thyroid enlargement with or without functional abnormality, presenting as solitary or multinodular goitre
Nutritional iodine deficiency; Genetic predisposition and locally autonomous nodular disease
Visible neck swelling; May produce compressive symptoms (dysphagia, dyspnea, stridor); Cosmetic concerns
Ultrasound differentiates solid versus cystic components, calcification, and elastography characteristics; FNAC for cytological evaluation; Isotope scanning for functional mapping
Thyroid suppression therapy (thyroxine) for benign cases; Hemithyroidectomy or total thyroidectomy for suspicious features
Distinguish from thyroid carcinoma via FNAC and targeted imaging; Exclude thyroiditis by ultrasound texture and antibody markers

Graveâ€™s Disease
Diffuse toxic goitre with autoimmune hyperfunction often accompanied by ophthalmopathy
Autoimmune etiology; Frequently in young to middle-aged patients
Features of hyperthyroidism with diffuse, vascular gland enlargement; May have ocular involvement (exophthalmos)
TFTs confirm hyperthyroidism; Ultrasound shows a hypervascular gland; Isotope scan if needed
Medical stabilization with beta blockers and antithyroid medications; Radioiodine therapy or near-total/total thyroidectomy based on patient factors
Exclude toxic multinodular goitre via imaging; Confirm diffuse gland involvement
Risk of thyroid storm if inadequately controlled; Post-therapeutic hypothyroidism and recurrent ophthalmopathy
Recurrent Goitre
Regrowth of thyroid tissue after previous surgery or treatment
Previous thyroid surgery with persistent or regrown tissue due to surgical scarring; Increased operative risks from distorted anatomy
Re-emergence of neck swelling possibly with compressive symptoms; Higher risk profile for nerve injury
Repeat ultrasound and imaging to assess anatomical distortion and lymph node involvement
Consider thyroid suppression or radioiodine therapy; Reoperation reserved for severe symptomatic cases
Exclude residual disease with imaging and selective FNAC sampling
Increased risk of recurrent laryngeal nerve injury and hypocalcemia due to scar tissue
Primary HPT
Excess parathyroid hormone secretion from one or more parathyroid glands causing hypercalcemia
Most commonly a solitary adenoma; Parathyroid hyperplasia or carcinoma less frequent; Genetic predispositions may play a role
Symptoms related to hypercalcemia (‘stones, bones, groans, and psychiatric overtones’); May be asymptomatic in mild cases
Elevated serum PTH and calcium, low phosphate, increased alkaline phosphatase; Localization studies with ultrasound, CT, MRI or Sestamibi scan
Surgical excision (adenoma removal); Subtotal parathyroidectomy with autotransplantation in hyperplasia; Total parathyroidectomy in carcinoma with possible thyroid and lymph node dissection

Postoperative hypocalcemia (hungry bone syndrome); Recurrent or persistent hyperparathyroidism if resection is incomplete
Secondary HPT
Parathyroid hyperplasia as a compensatory response to chronic hypocalcemia, often seen in chronic renal failure
Chronic renal failure; Prolonged vitamin D deficiency; Certain drug exposures
Mildly elevated calcium with high PTH; Bone pain, soft tissue calcifications, renal osteodystrophy
High PTH, low/normal calcium, high phosphate; Impaired renal function on laboratory tests
Correction of the underlying cause; Surgical intervention (subtotal or total parathyroidectomy with autotransplantation) for symptomatic cases

Progressive bone disease and vascular calcifications if untreated
Tertiary HPT
Autonomous parathyroid hyperfunction following long-term secondary stimulation
Longstanding renal failure after correction of the primary cause
Persistent hypercalcemia despite treatment for secondary causes; Worsening bone disease
Biochemical profile similar to primary HPT with history of chronic renal failure; Localization studies for surgical planning
Surgical intervention (subtotal or total parathyroidectomy with autotransplantation), often delayed until post-transplant stability
Differentiate from secondary HPT by persistence of hypercalcemia after primary correction
Severe hypercalcemia with bone demineralization and renal calcifications

Altered breast tissue involution and development; hormonal imbalance and cyclic estrogen/progesterone effects; local factors: trauma, infection (mastitis), ductal stasis; chronic inflammation leading to fibrosis and epithelial hyperplasia

Ageâ€‘specific occurrences (fibroadenoma in early reproductive years; cystic changes in perimenopause); ovarian hormone fluctuations (menstrual cycle, pregnancy, lactation); exogenous hormone exposure (oral contraceptives); smoking association (especially in duct ectasia)

Palpable mass: firm, mobile (fibroadenoma) or cystic, fluctuant (cysts); nipple discharge: bilateral, milky (physiologic during lactation) vs. unilateral, bloody/serous/greenish (suggestive of pathologic processes like duct ectasia); mastalgia: cyclical (preâ€‘menses) or nonâ€‘cyclical (burning quality); occasional skin changes (dimpling, retraction) and signs of inflammation (mastitis)

Mammography: detects microcalcifications, stellate masses, tissue asymmetry, guides sampling; ultrasound: differentiates solid vs. cystic lesions, ideal for dense breasts, assists in interventional procedures; MRI: used in highâ€‘risk individuals or implant evaluation; ductography/ductoscopy: visualizes duct architecture (papilloma vs. malignant features); tissue sampling: fine needle aspiration cytology and core biopsy for confirmation

Imageâ€‘guided interventions: ultrasound aspiration for cysts; cryoablation for small fibroadenomas; pharmacological options: NSAIDs or topical agents for mastalgia, evening primrose oil, danazol, lowâ€‘dose tamoxifen for cyclic pain (noting possible relapse upon cessation); targeted duct interventions: localized duct excision (microdochectomy) when discharge is confined; inflammatory conditions (mastitis/abscess): intravenous antibiotics (penicillin/cephalosporins) followed by interventional drainage if an abscess develops

Fibroadenoma vs. Carcinoma: mobile, wellâ€‘circumscribed mass with benign imaging features, confirmed via tissue sampling; mastalgia: cyclical pain lacking discrete mass and normal imaging excludes malignancy; nipple discharge: bilateral, milky secretion (lactation context) vs. unilateral, focal duct abnormality with bloody or serous fluid; fat necrosis: history of trauma with characteristic calcifications (oil cyst appearance) on imaging; duct ectasia: smoking history, duct dilation, and greenish/brown discharge favor a benign process

Recurrence of cysts after aspiration; abscess formation or antibiotic failure progressing to chronic infection; antibioma formation (indurated mass post pusâ€‘resorption); fistula formation or scarring in persistent duct ectasia

Malignant neoplasm arising from epithelial tissue; includes carcinoma in situ (DCIS, LCIS) and invasive types (commonly invasive ductal carcinoma, also lobular and inflammatory variants); most common cancer in women; rare in males

Multifactorial origin with genetic (BRCA1/BRCA2 mutations) and environmental influences; progression from precursor lesions (e.g., DCIS) with LCIS as an indicator of increased risk; estrogenâ€‘driven tumor development and progression

Predominantly female; male cases <0.5%; increasing age, majority seen in perimenopausal/postmenopausal patients; genetic predisposition (family history, BRCA mutations); hormonal factors (early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity, prolonged hormone therapy); obesity (enhanced estrogen conversion in adipose tissue), highâ€‘fat diet, alcohol intake; prior breast lesions (atypical hyperplasia); radiation exposure

Palpable, hard, irregular mass (often in the upper outer quadrant); skin changes: dimpling, retraction, â€˜peau dâ€™orangeâ€™, ulceration or indurated plaques (cancer en cuirasse); nipple alterations: retraction and/or discharge (may be bloody or clear); Pagetâ€™s disease: unilateral, eczematous nipple changes with confirmed Paget cells on biopsy; regional lymphadenopathy (axillary nodes); inflammatory variant: diffuse erythema, edema, and brawny induration, may present as stage IIIB; occasional presentation by symptoms of distant metastases

Mammography: identifies microcalcifications (common in DCIS), stellate masses, and asymmetry; ultrasound: characterizes lesions and directs sampling procedures; MRI: maps tumor extent in multifocal disease and evaluates highâ€‘risk patients; tissue sampling: FNAC, core (truâ€‘cut) biopsy, or excisional biopsy for definitive diagnosis; staging: TNM classification with adjunct imaging (CT, PET, bone scans) for metastases evaluation

Surgical procedures: breastâ€‘conserving surgery (wide local excision/quadrantectomy with adjuvant radiotherapy), mastectomy options (simple/total, modified radical with axillary dissection, with sentinel lymph node biopsy guidance); systemic therapies: chemotherapy (anthracyclines, taxanes, cyclophosphamide, methotrexate, 5â€‘fluorouracil) in neoadjuvant/adjuvant settings, hormonal agents (tamoxifen for receptorâ€‘positive cancers; aromatase inhibitors in postmenopausal patients), targeted therapy (trastuzumab for HER2â€‘overexpression with preâ€‘treatment cardiologic evaluation), endocrine ablation (surgical or medical oophorectomy in selected premenopausal cases); radiotherapy: postâ€‘surgical application to reduce local recurrence; palliative interventions: procedures to relieve metastatic complications (e.g., stenting, pleurodesis, bisphosphonates for bone lesions)

Inflammatory breast cancer vs. mastitis: lack of response to antibiotics, persistent induration and edema with biopsy revealing lymphatic invasion; Pagetâ€™s disease vs. benign nipple dermatoses: unilateral nipple changes resistant to topical treatment, confirmed by identification of Paget cells with immunohistochemistry; carcinoma vs. benign masses (e.g., fibroadenoma, fibrocystic change): irregular lesion margins, clusters of microcalcifications on imaging, definitive pathological features; male breast cancer vs. gynecomastia: focal, hard, fixed mass with nipple retraction and skin involvement versus diffuse, bilateral soft tissue proliferation on imaging

Local recurrence after breastâ€‘conserving approaches; regional lymph node involvement with risk for distant metastases (bone, lung, liver, brain); surgeryâ€‘related issues: seroma, hematoma, infection, nerve injury (e.g., long thoracic, thoracodorsal), lymphedema; systemic treatment complications: myelosuppression, cardiotoxicity (trastuzumab), thromboembolic risks, osteoporosis, endometrial effects; psychosocial and functional challenges following extensive surgical procedures

Fibroadenoma vs. Carcinoma: mobile, smooth, wellâ€‘demarcated lesions on ultrasound, tissue sampling confirms benign cytologic/histologic features; mastalgia: cyclical pain without detectable mass and normal imaging profile excludes cancer; nipple discharge: bilateral, milky secretions (lactationâ€‘associated) versus unilateral, bloody/serous discharge with localized duct abnormality indicative of pathology; fat necrosis: history of trauma with classic fatâ€‘density changes and coarse calcifications distinguishing it from neoplasia; duct ectasia: smoking history and duct enlargement with greenish/brown discharge support benign ductal changes

Minor Salivary Gland Disorders
Extravasation Cysts (Mucoceles)
Mucous collection within soft tissues following rupture of minor gland ducts.
Local trauma (e.g., accidental lip biting, blunt injury).
Frequent minor trauma; repetitive mechanical injuries on the lower lip.
Soft, fluctuant swelling (commonly on lower lip); may be painful or asymptomatic.
Ultrasound to demonstrate cystic nature if needed; observation for spontaneous resolution; surgical excision for persistent lesions.
History of trauma and typical location help distinguish from other mucosal cysts.
Recurrence with incomplete removal; potential secondary infection.
Minor Salivary Gland Disorders
Tumors of Minor Salivary Glands
Neoplastic growths arising from minor gland tissue; majority are malignant.
Idiopathic, with possible genetic predispositions.
Advanced age; occasional prior radiation exposure.
Benign: slow, painless, mobile mass. Malignant: firm mass, possible ulceration, local invasion.
Excisional or incisional biopsy based on size; imaging (CT/MRI) for lesion delineation; benign: local excision with clear margins; malignant: wide surgical excision (often with reconstruction).
Persistence and absence of acute inflammation distinguish from cystic lesions; histopathology confirms neoplastic character.
Local tissue invasion, recurrence, regional metastasis (in malignant cases).
Sublingual Salivary Gland Disorders
Mucous Retention Cysts and Plunging Ranula
Mucous retention within the duct system; a plunging ranula extends through the mylohyoid into the neck.
Ductal disruption from trauma leading to mucus accumulation.
Prior trauma; inherent anatomical predisposition to mucous pooling.
Soft, fluctuant swelling in the floor of the mouth; dumbbellâ€‘shaped if extending into the neck.
Ultrasound or CT scan demonstrating a cystic lesion with extension through the mylohyoid; complete surgical excision of the cyst tract to prevent recurrence.
Imaging confirms extension pattern, differentiating it from simple intraoral mucoceles or other cystic lesions.
Incomplete removal may lead to recurrence; risk of infection in persistent cases.
Sublingual Salivary Gland Disorders
Tumors of the Sublingual Gland
Neoplastic lesions within the sublingual gland, with most being malignant.
Primarily idiopathic; exact pathogenetic mechanisms remain unclear.
Typically older patients; potential correlation with previous risk exposures.
Rapidly enlarging mass in the floor of the mouth with possible pain and invasion of surrounding tissues.
CT/MRI for assessing extent; fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) for preliminary diagnosis; wide surgical excision with possible neck dissection.
Distinguishable from benign cysts by irregular borders, rapid growth on imaging and cytological features.
High risk of local invasion, metastasis, and recurrence if resection is incomplete.
Submandibular Salivary Gland Disorders
Acute Sialadenitis
Sudden inflammatory condition of the submandibular gland.
Bacterial infections often secondary to ductal obstruction; may follow a viral illness.
Dehydration; factors predisposing to duct obstruction.
Rapid onset of pain and gland swelling, often worsens during meals.
Ultrasound/CT demonstrating gland enlargement and inflammation; antibiotic therapy and supportive treatment.
Resolution with antibiotics and imaging findings help distinguish from viral or neoplastic causes.
Abscess formation; potential progression to chronic sialadenitis if inadequately managed.
Submandibular Salivary Gland Disorders
Chronic Sialadenitis
Longstanding inflammation, often due to recurrent duct obstruction from salivary stones.
Repeated episodes of obstruction from calculi leading to chronic inflammation.
High mucin concentration; dehydration; ductal anomalies.
Recurrent, mealâ€‘related painful swelling; palpable enlarged gland; sometimes a palpable stone.
CT/MRI, sialography, and ultrasound revealing calculi and chronic inflammatory changes; marsupialisation or gland excision in persistent cases.
Direct visualization of calculi and imaging exclude neoplastic processes.
Formation of abscesses; gland fibrosis leading to persistent discomfort.
Submandibular Salivary Gland Disorders
Tumors of the Submandibular Gland
Neoplastic lesions in the submandibular gland, with roughly half being malignant.
Primarily idiopathic; spontaneous neoplastic transformation is implicated.
Older age; potential history of radiation exposure.
Painless, slow-growing mass â€“ benign tumors are soft and well-circumscribed; malignant lesions are firmer and may invade adjacent tissue.
CT/MRI to outline extent; FNAC for cytological assessment; surgical excision ranging from intracapsular removal (small lesions) to complete gland excision with neck dissection (for malignant tumors).
Imaging and FNAC help exclude reactive adenopathy and inflammatory causes based on growth rate and lesion consistency.
Risk of recurrence, nerve injury, and local/regional spread in malignant cases.
Parotid Gland Disorders
Inflammatory Conditions
Acute inflammation of the parotid gland, which may be viral (e.g., mumps), bacterial, or obstructive in nature.
Viral pathogens (mumps), bacterial infections secondary to obstructive processes, or ductal stones.
Exposure to viral pathogens; dehydration; conditions predisposing to duct obstruction.
Unilateral or bilateral parotid swelling; pain more common in bacterial infection; exacerbation during meals in obstructive cases.
Ultrasonography and sialography revealing gland enlargement and duct dilatation; antibiotic therapy and supportive management for bacterial cases; supportive care for viral infections.
Rapid improvement with conservative management and typical imaging patterns distinguish these from neoplastic masses.
Abscess formation; persistent gland dysfunction if inflammation is unresolved.
Parotid Gland Disorders
Neoplastic Tumors
Tumors of the parotid gland, ranging from benign (most commonly pleomorphic adenoma) to various malignant types.
Mostly idiopathic; some association with prior ionizing radiation exposure.
Advanced age; certain environmental exposures.
Benign: slow, painless, smoothly contoured mass; malignant: may exhibit rapid growth, pain, and possible nodal involvement.

CT/MRI to determine tumor extent and relation to adjacent structures; FNAC to assess cytological features; benign lesions: superficial parotidectomy with careful preservation of facial nerve branches; malignant lesions: radical parotidectomy with neck dissection.
Growth rate, imaging characteristics (irregular margins/invasion), and FNAC findings allow differentiation from inflammatory or benign conditions.
Facial nerve injury, tumor recurrence, and risk of regional metastasis in malignant disease.
Tumor-like Lesions and Systemic Conditions
Sialadenosis
Diffuse, bilateral, non-inflammatory enlargement of salivary glands related to systemic/metabolic disturbances.
Metabolic or endocrine imbalances, including diabetes, chronic alcoholism, pregnancy, and bulimia.
Presence of an underlying systemic disorder affecting gland metabolism.
Painless, symmetric gland enlargement without focal masses or significant tenderness.
Ultrasonography demonstrating diffuse gland enlargement; laboratory evaluations to identify systemic disorders; management focuses on treating the underlying metabolic/endocrine condition.
Lack of focal mass on imaging and correlation with systemic workup excludes neoplastic or localized inflammatory causes.
Persistent cosmetic or functional issues if the primary metabolic disturbance remains uncorrected.
Tumor-like Lesions and Systemic Conditions
SjÃ¶gren Syndrome
Autoimmune-mediated progressive lymphocytic destruction of salivary and lacrimal glands.
Autoimmune response affecting glandular tissue; part of a broader spectrum of autoimmune disorders.
More common in middle-aged women; association with other autoimmune diseases.
Marked dryness of the mouth (xerostomia), possible gland enlargement, oral mucosal atrophy, increased susceptibility to candidiasis and dental caries.

Sialography, scintigraphy, and sialochemistry to document gland dysfunction; labial/minor gland biopsy revealing lymphocytic infiltration; serologic markers (autoantibodies) support the diagnosis; systemic immunomodulatory therapy (corticosteroids, cytotoxic agents) and supportive measures.
Diffuse gland involvement with characteristic serologic and biopsy findings distinguishes SjÃ¶gren syndrome from localized neoplasms.
Increased risk of lymphoma development; chronic dental and mucosal complications related to persistent xerostomia.

Esophageal Atresia/Tracheoesophageal Fistula (EA/TEF)
Clinical Definition
- Difficulty or delay in swallowing food/liquids - Involvement of one or more phases (oral, pharyngeal, esophageal)
- Chronic reflux of acidic gastric contents into the esophagus - Frequent reflux leading to mucosal injury
- Congenital interruption of the esophagus - May include an abnormal connection (fistula) between the trachea and esophagus
Causes

- Neurologic/central disorders (e.g., Alzheimerâ€™s, brain tumors) - Neuromuscular/muscular disorders - Endocrine/metabolic derangements and medication side effects - Motility disorders (e.g., achalasia, diffuse esophageal spasm) - Structural lesions (e.g., Zenker diverticulum, strictures, tumors) - Psychogenic factors
- Lower esophageal sphincter (LES) dysfunction (transient relaxations, low pressure) - Delayed gastric emptying; hiatal hernia - Impaired esophageal clearance
- Developmental malformation of the esophagus - Maternal exposures (methimazole, diabetes, thalidomide) - Multifactorial etiology (genetic predisposition)
Risk Factors

- In pediatrics: prematurity, neurological impairments (e.g., cerebral palsy) - Congenital anomalies (choanal atresia, cleft lip/palate, craniofacial syndromes) - In older patients: age-related reduction in muscle strength, poor dentition, decreased laryngeal elevation
- Obesity/increased intraâ€‘abdominal pressure - Presence of hiatal hernia; pregnancy - Lifestyle triggers (alcohol, spicy/acidic foods) - Medications that lower sphincter tone
- Maternal factors (drug exposure, diabetes) - Family history and frequent associated congenital anomalies (cardiac, vertebral, limb, renal)
Clinical Features

- Oral/Pharyngeal subset:  - Difficulty initiating swallow, coughing, choking  - Sensation of food sticking in throat; nasal regurgitation  - Wet voice; compensatory eating behaviors; weight loss - Esophageal type:  - Sensation of food sticking in lower throat/chest  - May be accompanied by heartburn-like symptoms
- Typical symptoms:  - Heartburn, acid regurgitation  - Dysphagia (sensation of food sticking) - Atypical/extraesophageal:  - Chronic cough, hoarseness, nonâ€‘cardiac chest pain, dental erosion

- Prenatal indicators:  - Polyhydramnios; absent/small stomach bubble on ultrasound - Postnatal findings:  - Drooling, choking/coughing with feeds  - Abdominal distension; risk for chemical pneumonitis
